welcome: Hi, and welcome to the AI Activation Program for Public Sector Sales. Here's the whole idea in one breath: one short activity a day, fifteen to twenty minutes, for four weeks, with Thanksgiving week off. That's it. You don't need to prepare, you don't need to catch up on everything at once, and you don't need to be an AI expert. Each day, open today's card, read the three or four steps, do them with Copilot, and post one short share in the Viva Engage channel. Week one sharpens how you use AI and how you judge what it gives you. Week two, you research one real account and build a small source pack. Week three, you turn that pack into your own Copilot agent. Week four, you use the agent to plan the account and rehearse a business review. The weeks build on each other, so just show up for today's step. If something gets stuck, bring it to the weekly coaching session. Don't overthink it. Fifteen minutes, one focused improvement, and you're done for the day.
w1-mon: Day one, The Challenger. Pick one claim you make all the time. Something like, we keep this agency's mission running, or, our campus connection speeds up research. Now ask Copilot to play a skeptical stakeholder, a contracting officer, a CIO, whoever usually pushes back, and have it find three weak points in that claim. Don't argue with it yet. Read the three, pick the one that would hurt most in a real meeting, and rewrite that claim using only evidence you actually have today. Then share three things: the weak claim, your rewrite, and the evidence you still need. Fifteen minutes. The skill here is simple: use AI to attack your idea, not to agree with it.
w1-tue: Day two, The Translator. Take one message, maybe yesterday's rewritten claim, or an update you need to send this week. Before you rewrite anything, ask Copilot to profile three readers: a customer leader, a technical stakeholder, and a partner lead. What does each one care about, what worries them, how do they judge success. Label which priorities are inferred, because Copilot is guessing. Then ask for three versions of your message, one per reader, with the same facts in every version. Finish by choosing one relevant question for each audience. Share the two versions that differ most and the difference that matters. For example, the leader version might lead with mission continuity, while the technical version leads with the connection design.
w1-wed: Day three, Make the Complex Simple. Pick a technical idea you explain a lot, interconnection is a good one. Ask Copilot for a few short analogies aimed at a nontechnical stakeholder. Then the important part: ask Copilot where each analogy breaks down. Every analogy bends somewhere. Pick the one that survives best and refine it against an approved reference, so it stays accurate. Share your clear explanation and the one limitation it must preserve. Example: if you compare interconnection to a private road between two buildings, the limitation might be that it's about direct, dedicated connections, not about the speed of any single car.
w1-thu: Day four, Reverse Engineer the Prompt. Start with a strong account preparation example, a brief you'd be happy to send. Paste it into Copilot and ask it to write the prompt that would produce something that good: who it's for, what evidence it may use, which unknowns it must list rather than guess, the tone, and the next action it should end with. Now test that prompt on a different agency, institution, or partner scenario and see what breaks. Fix one thing. Share your reusable prompt and the one improvement from the test. You're building a tool you'll use every week, so keep it to one screen.
w1-fri: Day five, The Situation Room. This is where the week comes together. Take a messy situation: price pressure, incomplete customer information, and a partner who isn't aligned. Use what you practiced this week. Challenge the assumptions, compare how the customer, the partner, and your own leadership see it, and then decide. Write a three sentence brief and two coordinated next actions, one toward the customer and one toward the partner. Share the brief, the two actions, and what changed your thinking. If both actions point at the customer, that's a sign to go back and give the partner one of them.
w2-mon: Week two, day one. Choose the Account and Research Questions. Pick one real account, an agency, an institution, or a partner supported customer, the one you'll carry for the rest of the program. Write three questions about its priorities, its challenges, and its future plans. For example: what is the agency's modernization priority this year, when is the next recompete window, which partner is already in the account. Find one authoritative source, a strategic plan, a budget document, a public announcement, and start a source register with it. Keep it small: one account, one useful sales conversation. Share the account, your three questions, and that first source.
w2-tue: Week two, day two. Build the Customer Source Pack. Today you collect a small set of documents or permitted excerpts about your account: customer plans, technical or service needs, funding or procurement signals, and partner involvement where there's evidence. For each one, record where it came from, when it was published, when you accessed it, and why it matters. You're aiming for three to five good sources across the week, not twenty. Share your source register and one representative finding, something like, the agency's plan names network modernization as a priority for the next two years.
w2-wed: Week two, day three. Find the Customer and Partner Story. Give Copilot your pack and ask it to connect the findings: customer priorities, stakeholder interests, partner contributions, and where Equinix might be relevant. Use approved capability references for any product claim. The one rule: keep what the sources actually say separate from your own opportunity hypothesis. Share three findings with their sources, and one hypothesis. For example: finding, the university received a research computing grant; hypothesis, that research may need a private connection to a cloud provider, which we should ask about.
w2-thu: Week two, day four. Challenge the Intelligence. Ask Copilot to argue against the account story you've built. What's missing, what contradicts, what's stale. Then check your most important claims against the original documents, not against Copilot's summary. Refine the pack and turn anything unresolved into discovery questions you can actually ask. Share one claim you corrected or qualified, and the questions that remain. A typical catch: a funding figure from an older document that's since been revised.
w2-fri: Week two, day five. Create the Account Brief. Pull the week into one page: priorities, stakeholders and partners, potential value, alternatives, unknowns, and next questions. Then finalize the pack with a contents list and five test questions for your agent next week: two with known answers, one that needs synthesis, one where the information is missing, and one that's outside the account altogether. Share the one page brief and the pack contents list. Then save everything in its approved location. You get a week off, and this pack is what you'll build the agent from when you come back.
w3-mon: Week three, day one. Understand and Design Your Agent. Welcome back. Start by watching the first two minutes of the Microsoft Mechanics video, right from the card. Then design before you build: what is the agent for, who will use it, which three account tasks should it handle, and how should it answer. Pick which files from your pack support those tasks. Draft the instructions: use evidence, label assumptions, say when information is missing, and keep customer and partner perspectives separate. Share your short agent design and the draft instructions. Example task: prepare me for a meeting with the agency's program office.
w3-tue: Week three, day two. Build Your Account Agent. Watch the two assigned chapters, about four minutes, then go into Agent Builder in Microsoft 365 Copilot. Create the agent, check its name and instructions, add your Customer Source Pack through the approved knowledge setup, and add three starter prompts. Confirm the sources are ready, then ask one question you already know the answer to and see whether the agent finds it in your pack. Share the setup and that first checked response. If the agent can't see your files yet, that's today's finding, not a failure. Bring it to coaching.
w3-wed: Week three, day three. Test What It Knows. Watch the two short testing chapters, then run the five questions you wrote in week two. For each one, check whether the agent cited your sources, got the facts right, synthesized when it had to, and admitted when the information was missing. Mark each response pass or issue, and pick the single most important fix. Share the test record and that top issue. Example: the agent answered the missing information question with a confident guess instead of saying it didn't know. That's the fix for tomorrow.
w3-thu: Week three, day four. Improve and Maintain Your Agent. Watch the short chapter on editing an agent, then fix yesterday's top issue, in the instructions or in the source content, and rerun the failed test. Next, add one verified account update or correct an existing source, refresh the knowledge, and confirm the agent uses the new version. Finally, write down who owns updates and when the next review is. Share the correction, the retest result, and your update routine. An agent that nobody maintains is out of date in a month, so this step matters as much as the build.
w3-fri: Week three, day five. Put Your Agent to Work. Watch the sharing chapter, then use your agent for real: prepare a customer or partner conversation. Ask it for priorities, questions to raise, and next actions. Demonstrate the result. If sharing is enabled and appropriate in your tenant, let a colleague try it and confirm they can access the knowledge. Share a short demonstration, the prompts that worked, and the limitations that remain. Keep this agent and this pack, because next week you'll use them for strategy.
w4-mon: Week four, day one. Establish the Account Truth. Open your agent and ask it to review the account: customer priorities, recent developments, relationship gaps, and unanswered questions. Then ask it to separate evidence from inference, and to say what matters most for the next conversation. Pick the single most consequential finding and verify it yourself against the source pack. Share three strategic findings, each with the evidence or the gap behind it. For example: finding, the recompete is eighteen months out; evidence, the agency's acquisition forecast; gap, we don't know who the new program manager is.
w4-tue: Week four, day two. Develop the Account Strategy. Work with your agent to shape the priorities: retention, growth, and the relationship, wherever each applies. For each one include the customer outcome, the partner's contribution, a proposed owner, milestones, and how you'll measure success. Then challenge one assumption that could stall the plan. Ask the agent, what has to be true for this to work. Share a concise account or joint partner plan and the one risk you addressed. If every owner on the plan is you, bring the partner in.
w4-wed: Week four, day three. Explore the Scenarios. Ask your agent how the strategy changes if funding is delayed, if connectivity demand changes, or if the partner's role is different. Compare a baseline with two changes. Label every hypothetical input as a scenario, not a forecast. If you use numbers or projections, check the calculations in an approved spreadsheet and keep the assumptions with them. Share a simple comparison table and one implication for the plan. Example: if the grant slips a quarter, the first milestone moves, so the discovery meeting should happen before the funding decision, not after.
w4-thu: Week four, day four. Rehearse the Business Review. Ask the same agent to play three people: a customer leader, a technical stakeholder, and a partner executive. Invite the hard questions, on value, delivery, cost, evidence, and who is responsible for what. Answer them briefly. Then ask the agent which answer was weakest, and improve that one. Sharpen the decision or commitment you'll ask for at the end of the real review. Share the hardest question and your improved answer. A shorter, clearer answer usually beats a longer one.
w4-fri: Week four, day five, the last one. Build the Forward Looking Business Review. Use your agent and the week's work to assemble a concise customer QBR or partner business review: what changed, why it matters, future priorities, what the scenarios imply, and the actions you propose. Put it into a short document or your existing review template. Share the review and the decisions it's designed to support. And that's the program: a sharper message, a real source pack, a working agent, and a review you could take into a real conversation next quarter. Nicely done.
